title: Manu and the little fish
hookLine: a tiny fish begs Manu for protection, and the Arthashastra names the law of the fish
carry: raja dharma: power exists to protect the small
tomorrow: same whistle, three referees. which one do people trust?

lines: PROTECT ME, SAYS THE LITTLE FISH.
THE FISH SAVES MANU FROM THE FLOOD.
cards: Manu is at a riverbank when a tiny fish speaks to him. Protect me, it says. The big fish eat the small ones; that's the way of our kind.
So Manu scoops it into a jar. It grows, and he moves it to a pond, then to the Ganga, then to the sea. And when the great flood comes, that fish, now enormous and horned, tows Manu's boat to safety.
In the Mahabharata it reveals itself as Brahma; in the Puranas it's Matsya, Vishnu's first avatar. Every telling starts the same way: a small fish afraid of the big ones, and someone who takes it in.

teach.h: MATSYA NYAYA: THE LAW OF THE FISH.
teach.b: That fear has a name in Sanskrit: matsya nyaya, the law of the fish. The Arthashastra, this week's handbook on government, reaches for it to answer a plain question: why should anyone hold power?
Its word for power is danda, the rod, a ruler's power to restrain and punish.

teach.h: NO ROD: THE STRONG SWALLOW THE WEAK.
teach.b: Where no rod is held, it says, the law of the fish takes over, and the strong swallow the weak. Where the rod is held, the weak can stand their ground. Look at who the argument is for.
Not the king's comfort, not his glory: the small fish.

Hindu tradition calls a ruler's duty raja dharma, and its first word is protection. The Mahabharata's long teaching on kingship says it too: without a king, people would devour one another like fish in water.
And many teachers read the flood story the same way.

teach.h: THE ONE HE SAVED WAS DIVINE.
teach.b: Before Manu is anyone's ruler or lawgiver, he takes in a fish too small to save itself, and the one he protects turns out to be divine. Readers argue about how well the rest of the Arthashastra lives up to that picture.
Power that doesn't guard the small is just a bigger fish.

how: Hindus honor Matsya as Vishnu's first avatar, and many families make a small daily offering to birds and animals; the Arthashastra's picture of danda and the law of the fish is studied as a classic of Indian thought on government.

o: an old ruling book's promise of glory to a strong king
an old ruling book's reason for power: to guard the small
an old ruling book's plan for winning wars with spies

games.q: the fish and the rod — tap the pairs.
p: begged Manu for protection from the big ones
the fish, honored as Vishnu's first avatar
the law of the fish: the strong swallow the weak
the rod, held so the weak can stand

s: the Arthashastra says power exists for the king's glory
its first reason is the law of the fish: without the rod, the strong swallow the weak.
Manu took in a small fish afraid of the big ones
jar, pond, river, sea; then the fish towed his boat through the flood.
the law of the fish means fair play among equals
it's the opposite: a world with no rule, where the big eat the small.

games.q: on your block, a few big households park across everyone's driveways because nobody ever objects. the neighbors ask you to help write a parking rule. by the law of the fish, what's the rule for?
o: to keep the peace by asking the big households nicely, and nothing more.
to protect the ones who'd lose out without it, with a way to enforce it.
to punish the big households, so the strong finally lose for once.
games.why: raja dharma starts with protection. the Arthashastra's case for the rod is that without it the strong swallow the weak; its aim is that the weak can stand their ground, not revenge on the strong.

practice: Many Hindu households feed the small every day: a handful of grain for the birds, a first roti for a cow or a dog. If you can, set out a little food or water for some small creature today.
If not, bring to mind one person near you who gets pushed aside, name one small step you could take for them, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: danda, the ruler's rod, held so the big fish don't eat the small.

orig.note: Sanskrit dandaniti, the guidance of the rod: in the Arthashastra, the art of government.

carryVoice: Your line: raja dharma, power exists to protect the small. Manu started with one fish. That's day fifteen eighty-seven.

sources.ref: Arthashastra 1.4 (danda and dandaniti; the law of the fish; the rod keeps the other sciences secure)

Mahabharata 3.185 (critical edition; Manu raises the fish from jar to pond to Ganga to sea; it tows his ship and reveals itself as Brahma)
Mahabharata 12.67 (Shanti Parva, raja dharma: without a king people devour one another like fish)
